title: The heart's look (Matthew 5:27–30)
hookLine: faithfulness starts in the eyes and the heart

cards: Every marriage, every friendship, every promise has a moment before the moment. Long before anyone does anything, there's a look that lingers. A daydream you keep returning to.
A thought you feed instead of letting go. Nobody else can see it. It feels private and harmless.
Jesus has followed thou shalt not kill back to anger. Now he takes another of the Ten Commandments and follows it back to the eyes.

teach.b: Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, thou shalt not commit adultery.

Then, in the King James Bible: "But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart." This isn't about noticing that someone is attractive.
The Greek phrase means looking at someone in order to desire them: a look with a purpose, fed on purpose.
And the verb for lust, epithumeo, is the same word the Greek Old Testament uses in the commandment against coveting: thou shalt not covet thy neighbor's wife.

So Jesus joins two commandments: the act and the wanting, the body and the heart. Faithfulness doesn't start at the door of a hotel room. It starts in what you let your eyes and your imagination rest on.
Then a startling image: if your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and throw it away. If your right hand does, cut it off.
Christian tradition reads this as vivid exaggeration, the way a teacher makes a point unforgettable, not as a literal instruction.

teach.h: THE EYE AND THE HAND: TAKE IT SERIOUSLY.
teach.b: It means: take this seriously. Be willing to cut off what feeds the wrong thing, whether an app, a habit, a late-night conversation or a way of looking. The same logic reaches far beyond marriage.
Envy, greed and resentment start the same way, with a look that lingers and gets fed. What you keep looking at, you start to want. What you want, you start to become.

how: Christians speak of guarding the heart and the eyes; in the Orthodox tradition this is called watchfulness, and some Christians examine what they've looked at and longed for in daily or weekly self-examination.

o: to desire or covet: a look fed on purpose
to break a marriage vow by an act
to notice that someone is attractive

p: the same verb as lust here
a vivid way to say: take it seriously

games.q: a thought you know you shouldn't feed keeps returning. nobody can see it. what's the teaching here?
o: faithfulness starts in what you let your heart feed on.
games.why: Jesus traces the act back to the heart: "hath committed adultery with her already in his heart." the look that's fed is where it starts.

practice: Think about where your eyes go when you're bored or tired: which feeds, which screens, which faces, which store windows, and notice one kind of looking that leaves you emptier, more envious or less faithful to someone.
Then picture the next hour, and your eyes resting somewhere else when that pull comes: the sky, a book, the person in front of you. If you pray, you can ask for a faithful heart.

wordCard.voice: Epithumeo, the Greek word for to desire, to covet, a look fed on purpose. Jesus traces unfaithfulness back from the act to the eyes and the heart.

orig.note: Greek: to desire, to covet. Matthew 5:28, the same verb as the Greek of thou shalt not covet.

carryVoice: Your line: faithful in the heart. Long before the act, there's the look. That's day two hundred forty-four.
